title: Framing: how can the same story sound different?
examples: What is framing in the media?
How can two headlines tell the same story differently?
How do words change how we feel about news?

explain.say: Here are two headlines about the same exam: "Nine in ten pupils pass" and "One in ten pupils fail". Same numbers! But do they feel the same? Look at the board. Two frames around one story, side by side.

explain.say: See frame A on the left? It talks about the nine who passed, uses hopeful words and a photo of smiling pupils. A frame is the way a story is shown: which facts go first, which words and pictures are used. How does frame A make you feel?

explain.say: Now look at frame B on the right. It talks about the one in ten who failed, with worried words and a photo of an empty desk. Nothing in it is false, yet it feels like bad news. Which headline would make you click?

explain.say: Framing is not always a trick: every story needs some frame, and both frames here are true. But it shapes how we feel and what we think should be done. Psychologists Tversky and Kahneman showed that people choose differently when the same facts are framed as gains or as losses. Can you reframe "the glass is half empty"?

explain.say: So when you read the news, ask: what is the frame here, and how else could this be told? Brilliant work! Challenge: take one news story and write two headlines for it, one hopeful and one worried, using only true facts.

faq.a: Framing is how a story is presented: which facts come first, what words, numbers and pictures are used, and what is left out. The same facts can be framed to feel hopeful or worrying.

faq.q: How does a positive frame change a story?
faq.a: A positive frame highlights successes and uses hopeful words and pictures, like "nine in ten pass". It can make people feel things are going well.

faq.q: How does a negative frame change a story?
faq.a: A negative frame highlights problems and losses, like "one in ten fail", with worried words and pictures. It can make the same facts feel like a crisis.

faq.q: Is framing the same as lying?
faq.a: No. Framing uses true facts but chooses how to present them. That can still mislead if important facts are left out, so it is worth looking at other frames too.

faq.q: What did Tversky and Kahneman find about framing?
faq.a: In 1981 they showed people chose differently between identical options when they were described as lives saved rather than lives lost. This is called the framing effect.

facts: Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described the framing effect in 1981 using their "Asian disease problem" experiment.
Daniel Kahneman won the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002, partly for this work on how people make decisions.

quiz.say: "90 percent fat free" and "contains 10 percent fat" describe the same yogurt. What is this an example of?
quiz.why: Both are true; they are framed to feel different.

wrong.2: Social proof is about copying others.
